issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette: Andreas had always been a private person, but after six months of being stalked by a former acquaintance, he found himself constantly on edge. The experience had left an indelible mark on his life, one that he struggled to shake off even two years later. As a tutor, Andreas worked with students in quiet, one-on-one settings, which suited him just fine. However, the stalking had made him acutely aware of his surroundings, and the sound of motorcycles outside his window or while walking to work would send his heart racing. He couldn't explain why, but the noise seemed to embody the same sense of unpredictability and menace that his stalker had represented. Andreas's mind often wandered back to the stalking, replaying moments when he felt like he was being watched or followed. Even now, when walking down a familiar street, he would catch himself scanning the crowds, searching for a glimpse of his stalker's face. This hypervigilance had become second nature, and Andreas couldn't shake off the feeling that he was constantly being tracked. It wasn't just the physical sensations that unsettled him; it was also the memories of how he felt during those six months – trapped, helpless, and completely at the mercy of his stalker. As a result, Andreas had developed some maladaptive coping strategies to deal with these feelings. He would often tell himself that he deserved to suffer because of what happened, that somehow he must have provoked the stalking or could have done something to prevent it. This self-blame manifested in subtle ways; for instance, when working with students, Andreas would be excessively critical of himself, as if trying to atone for some unknown sin. He also found it difficult to form close relationships, including with his wife, whom he loved dearly but struggled to open up to emotionally. The experience had left Andreas with a deep-seated mistrust of others and a pervasive sense of self-doubt. He couldn't shake off the feeling that people were hiding something from him or that they might turn against him at any moment. This wariness extended even to his students, whom he would sometimes find himself questioning about their true intentions. Andreas knew this wasn't rational, but the fear had become a constant companion, one that made it difficult for him to relax or feel truly safe. At night, these feelings of unease would intensify, making it hard for Andreas to fall asleep or stay asleep. He would lie awake, listening for any unusual sounds outside his window, convinced that someone was lurking just out of sight. His wife had tried to reassure him, but even her presence couldn't calm the racing thoughts that kept him up at night. Andreas's life had become a series of carefully constructed routines and avoidance strategies. He stuck to familiar places and avoided going anywhere new, always on the lookout for potential dangers or escape routes. Even simple tasks like grocery shopping became an ordeal, as he would find himself scanning the aisles for signs of trouble. Recently, however, Andreas's wife had sat him down and gently pointed out how his behavior was affecting their relationship and his overall well-being. She encouraged him to seek help, reminding him that he didn't have to face this alone. For the first time in two years, Andreas felt a glimmer of hope – maybe there was a way to break free from this prison of fear and mistrust. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but with his wife's support, he finally felt ready to confront the demons that had been haunting him for so long. As Andreas sat in the therapist's office, he couldn't help but feel a sense of trepidation. What if he wasn't strong enough to overcome these feelings? What if he would always be trapped by this constant threat monitoring and self-doubt? But as he looked around the quiet room, he felt a spark of determination ignite within him – maybe it was time to take control back and start rebuilding his life, one small step at a time.
